text:
A: Alright! Hiya. Can you hear me okay?
B: Hi, yeah. Erm, I'm Abena.
A: Callum. I'm in St Helens, near Liverpool. Where are you?
B: Chelmsford. In Essex.
A: Ah, nice. Is that a uni hoodie? Anglia Ruskin?
B: Yeah, I'm in first year. Biomedical science.
A: Proper science, that. What's that involve, like labs and microscopes?
B: Yeah, kind of. We do a lot of practicals, like blood samples, cell cultures. I want to go into haematology eventually, in an NHS lab. Erm, the vet I talked to earlier said I'd be getting her muddy cow samples, so.
A: Ha, was that Rebecca? I've not had her yet. I'm hoping she's next, she's got a lurcher and I've got a greyhound, Dolly, so we've got loads to talk about.
B: Oh, Moss. She stole a block of cheese.
A: Did she! Dolly wouldn't, she's too scared. She's scared of the hoover, she's scared of the kettle. Honestly, thirty kilos of dog hiding behind the settee from a Dyson.
B: [laughs] Oh no. Bless her.
A: She's fine, she's spoiled rotten. What do you do when you're not studying then? I saw the plants and the drawings.
B: Erm, I read a lot, and I draw. Those are botanical drawings, with fine-liners. And I watch science YouTube, like explainers and stuff.
A: Oh, I'm the same but with podcasts. I listen on the drive to work, I'm on shifts at the glassworks. Last week I did about four hours on the Moon landings. Did you know the computer on Apollo 11 had less memory than a calculator?
B: Yeah, I watched a video about that! And they kept getting alarms on the way down, like error codes, and they just kind of decided to keep going.
A: The 1202 alarm! Yeah! That's the bit I love. Some lad in mission control, about my age, has to go, it's fine, keep going. Imagine that being your call. I get a furnace alarm on nights and I feel the pressure, and that's just glass.
B: That's still quite a lot of pressure though. Like, a furnace.
A: Yeah, to be fair, it's fifteen hundred degrees. But you just stay calm, check your readings, do what you've been trained to do. Same as them really, just less famous.
B: I think that's the bit I worry about. Like, in a lab, if I got something wrong with someone's blood results. I check everything three times.
A: Three times is good! I'm the one who logs everything at work, the older lads take the mick out of me. But it's always the tidy handover that saves you, do you know what I mean.
B: Yeah. That makes me feel a bit better, actually.
A: Good. Sorry, can I ask, is that a cross on your necklace?
B: Oh, yeah. Erm, I go to church. Methodist. I sing in the youth choir. I saw the crucifix on your shelf, actually, in the photo.
A: Ah, yeah, that was me nan's. Catholic. I'm not, like, every Sunday, I go with me mum at Christmas and Easter and the odd one. It's sort of quiet but there, if that makes sense.
B: No, it does. That's kind of how it is for me. Like, I don't really talk about it, but when I'm anxious, before exams and stuff, it helps.
A: Yeah. When me nan died last year, honestly, it was the thing that got me through. Didn't expect it to.
B: I'm sorry. I lost my grandma too, a few years ago. In Ghana.
A: Ah, sorry. It's hard, isn't it. Were you close?
B: Yeah, I wish I'd visited more. Sorry, that's quite heavy.
A: Don't be sorry. Honestly, it's better than me banging on about pub quizzes, which is what I did last call.
B: [laughs] Pub quizzes?
A: Long story. I'm captain of a team, and the quizmaster had the Moon landing as—
